entries.topicDescription: Runtime application self-protection and obfuscation strategies.

tips.title: Hollow-shell pattern for RASP threat callbacks
tips.content:
Exposing your real ThreatEngine implementation as a keepClassMembers target
leaks its method structure to reverse engineers even under obfuscation,
since kept methods retain readable names and signatures.

Instead, expose a minimal hollow interface/shell class that DexGuard's runtime
hooks call into, and keep the actual detection logic in an internal,
fully-obfuscated implementation reached only through that shell — this is a
Proxy pattern applied specifically to minimize the attack surface exposed by
keep rules.

tips.title: R8 shrinks, obfuscates and optimizes — enable it for release builds
tips.content:
R8 does three jobs on a release build: it removes unused code and resources (shrinking), renames classes, methods and fields to short names (obfuscation), and rewrites code to make it smaller and faster (optimization). It only runs when you enable minification (isMinifyEnabled = true).

Use the optimizing default rules file, and keep your own rules in proguard-rules.pro. Always test the minified build, because most R8 problems (a removed or renamed class used by reflection) only appear at runtime.

tips.title: Keep the mapping file to read obfuscated crash reports
tips.content:
Obfuscation is what makes crash traces from release builds unreadable ("a.b.c.d(Unknown Source)"). R8 writes a mapping.txt for every build; with it you can translate a trace back to real names. Keep one per released version — a mapping from another build will produce wrong names.

Play Console and Crashlytics can deobfuscate automatically when they receive the mapping (for an AAB, Play uploads it with the bundle; Crashlytics has a Gradle plugin that uploads it).

tips.title: Write narrow keep rules, and only for code reached by reflection
tips.content:
R8 removes or renames anything it can't see being used. Code that is reached only through reflection, JNI, or names in a config file breaks in a minified build. Fix it with a keep rule — but keep the rule as narrow as possible, because a broad rule like -keep class com.example.** {*;} switches off shrinking and obfuscation for everything it matches.

Prefer the @Keep annotation on a specific class, or a targeted -keepclassmembers rule, and rely on library-provided consumer rules where available.

tips.title: Verify Play Integrity verdicts on your server, with a fresh nonce
tips.content:
The Play Integrity API returns a signed verdict about the device and the app. It only protects you if the decision is made server-side: a client that checks its own verdict can be patched to skip the check.

Have your server generate a unique nonce per request, bind it to the action being protected, pass it to the API, and then have your server decode and verify the returned token (including that the nonce matches) before trusting the request. Reject replayed or mismatched tokens.
tips.codeSnippet:
val integrityManager = IntegrityManagerFactory.create(context)

integrityManager.requestIntegrityToken(
    IntegrityTokenRequest.builder()
        .setNonce(nonceFromServer)   // unique, single-use, bound to this action
        .build()
).addOnSuccessListener { response ->
    sendToServer(response.token())   // the server decodes and verifies it
}
